title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 127
paragraphs: From Italy came Smindyrides son of Hippocrates of Sybaris, who of all men on earth had attained the highest degree of luxury (for Sybaris was at that time at the height of its prosperity), and Damasus of Siris, son of that Amyris who was called the Wise; these came from Italy. From the Ionian gulf came Amphimnestus son of Epistrophus of Epidamnus; from Aetolia came Males, the brother of that Titormus who surpassed all Greeks in strength and who fled the company of men to the remotest part of the Aetolian land. From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon the tyrant of the Argives — the Pheidon who established the standard weights and measures still used in the Peloponnese, and who outdid all other Greeks in outrageous arrogance, for he removed the Elean presidents of the games from their posts and presided over the Olympic games himself; I say, his son, and with him Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paios, the son of that Euphorion who, according to the Arcadian story, entertained the Dioscuri in his home and from then on made a point of welcoming everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaios of Elis — these came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, son of that Alcmaeon who had gone to Croesus, and with him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who surpassed the other Athenians in both wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.
